blocks.text: Propositional equivalence is a concept in propositional logic. It explains when two logical expressions have the same meaning. Even if expressions look different, they may give the same result. Propositional equivalence is checked using truth tables. If two expressions have the same truth values in all cases, they are equivalent. The symbol “≡” is used to show equivalence. Propositional equivalence improves clarity in reasoning (as shown in Figure 2.6).

blocks.alt: A framed figure: the line The following two propositional expressions are logically equivalent; Expression 1, (A AND NOT B) OR (B AND NOT A), and Expression 2, (A OR B) AND (NOT A OR NOT B), joined by a double arrow; the note Both expressions are true in the same cases (XOR). Below, a Venn diagram panel with A only and B only hatched and the overlap left white, and a Truth Table panel; at the bottom the Therefore line.
blocks.caption: Figure 2.6: Two logically equivalent propositional expressions, by Venn diagram and truth table (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 2.6).
blocks.long_description: Venn key: A AND NOT B (hatched beige); B AND NOT A (hatched blue); Neither A nor B (white); A AND B (not included) (hatched beige). Truth table rows (A, B, Expression 1, Expression 2): F F F F; F T T T; T F T T; T T F F. Therefore line: (A AND NOT B) OR (B AND NOT A), a double arrow, (A OR B) AND (NOT A OR NOT B).

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Equivalent expressions may look different but always give the same result; they help simplify complex logic.
